conditions: captive zoo birds: 22 penguins housed (11 Exhibit, 11 Off Exhibit); 12 birds took part in the kin versus non-kin test (9 Exhibit, 3 Off Exhibit) and 10 in the familiar versus unfamiliar non-kin test, with 10 birds in both (Methods, from a page summary, paraphrased); no separate blank control odour is described, the kin test paired odours of an unfamiliar kin (r = 0.125 to 0.5) and an unfamiliar non-kin ('odors from an unfamiliar kin (coefficient of relationship, r, = 0.125–0.5) and an unfamiliar non-kin'), so familiarity was matched; donors of each pair were the same sex and the observer was blind to odour placement and donor identity; latency to investigate non-kin odour was shorter but not significant (Z = 1.784, P = 0.074); in the familiar versus unfamiliar non-kin test, penguins spent more time inside kennels with the familiar odour (Wilcoxon Z = 1.992, P = 0.046, paraphrase); the abstract states 'In tests of kin recognition, penguins preferred unfamiliar non-kin odors.'; time inside kennels was also longer for non-kin than kin odour (t11 = 3.434, P = 0.006); the authors read the non-kin preference as novelty through phenotype matching (non-kin odours did not match the birds' recognition templates); all but one bird took the kin test first, about 77 days before the familiarity test, so test order was not counterbalanced; no effects of sex or mating status were found

source.title: Odor-Based Recognition of Familiar and Related Conspecifics: A First Test Conducted on Captive Humboldt Penguins (Spheniscus humboldti)
